Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Random Variable Probability Distribution SA: W03 1 / 50Reminder: Function
Functions are everywhere in mathematics and therefore in statistics
Recapitulate properties of functions which are most important for us
First: “oﬀicial” definition:
In mathematics, a function from a set X to a set Y assigns to
each element of Xexactly one element of Y.
The set X is called the domain of the function and the set Y is
called the codomain of the function.
This definition is quite abstract and general: Give an example
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Random Variable Probability Distribution SA: W03 2 / 50Example: Grades
Let Pbe number of points you can score in an exam, e.g.:
P=f0,1,2,. . . 20g
Usually , these will be translated in grades G, e.g., in Switzerland:
G=f1,1.5,. . . 6g
Some notation: Let pdenote points scored and gcorresponding grade
Afunction , denoted by f, assigns to each pcorresponding g:
f(p)= g
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Random Variable Probability Distribution SA: W03 3 / 50Variable p:Independent variable
Variable g:Dependent variable
Grade g depends on number of points p
For example:
f(0)= 1 oder f(20)= 6 oder f(12)= 4.5
Note: Did not specify so far how this assignment works

Not possible:
f(10)= 4 and f(10)= 3.5

One student would fail, but not the other one
Someone of you would quite rightly complain

In school and books: Functions are often denoted by y= f(x)or

Further notions about functions will be introduced as we go along
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Random Variable Probability Distribution SA: W03 8 / 50Random Variable: Example
Very important notion in statistics: Random variable
Pack of playing cards (Switzerland): 36 different cards, with 4 suits
and card values 6 ,7,8,9,10, Jack, Queen, King and Ace each
Draw three cards in a row, put them back into deck after each draw
Do this twice and get following results:
1 6, Queen, King
2 8, Jack, Ace
Question: Which result is “better”?
Hard to compare in this form
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Random Variable Probability Distribution SA: W03 9 / 50A solution: Assign numbers to individual playing cards:
▶6, 7, 8, 9 have value 0
▶10 has value 10
▶Jack has value 2
▶Queen has value 3
▶King has value 4
▶Ace has value 11
Now draws are comparable:
1 6, Queen, King :0+3+4= 7
2 8, Jack, Ace :0+2+11= 13
Second draw with these assigned values better than first
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Random Variable Probability Distribution SA: W03 10 / 50Random Variable
Example above: Situation occurs frequently in statistics
Random experiment with sample space Ω
Numbers are assigned to all elementary events of Ω
Every elementary event ω has a value
X(ω)= x
X:Function , which assigns number xto each elementary event ω
This function: Random variable
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Random Variable Probability Distribution SA: W03 11 / 50Example
Drawing cards from a deck of playing cards
Each card a number is assigned:
ω= Ace 7! X(ω)= 11
ω= King 7! X(ω)= 4
......
ω= Six 7! X(ω)= 0
With numbers X(ω), e.g. “average” of drawn cards can be calculated
Average of “6, Queen, King” equal to7
3
For elementary events “6”, “Queen” and “King” without numbers,
notion “average” makes no sense at all
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Random Variable Probability Distribution SA: W03 12 / 50Example
Roll a blue and red die together
Sample space Ω (see earlier): Numbers on dice:
Ω=f11,12,. . . 16,21,22,. . .,26,. . . 66g
Different random variables can be defined on Ω
Let Xbe random variable for sum of numbers:
▶Hence:
X(16)= 7 or X(31)= 4 or X(13)= 4
▶Values that random variable can take is called range :
W X=f2,3,4. . .,11,12g
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Random Variable Probability Distribution SA: W03 13 / 50Let Ybe number on red die:
▶Then:
Y(16)= 6 or Y(31)= 1 or Y(13)= 3
▶Range:
W Y=f1,2,. . .,6g
Let Zbe equal 0 for all elementary events:
▶Then:
Z(16)= 0 or Z(31)= 0 or Z(13)= 0
▶Range:
W Z=f0g
Last example is a completely legitimate random variable
How useful this is, is another question
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Random Variable Probability Distribution SA: W03 14 / 50Example
Randomly select a person
Sample space Ω:All people on this planet
Many random variables are conceivable:
▶X:Random variable that assigns income to each person
▶Y:Random variable that assigns height to each person
▶Z:Random variable that assigns age to each person
Following variables are not random variables:
▶Variable Vassigns gender to each person
▶Variable W assigns corresponding nationality to each person
“Result” of a random variable has to be anumber

R:Real numbers (points on number line, all decimal fractions)
Statistics X(or Y,Z,. . . ): Notation for random variables (functions )
Functions in mathematics often in form:
y= f(x)
Following distinction is very important:
▶Random variable are denoted by capital letters X(or Y,Z)
▶Corresponding lowercase letters x(or y,z) represents specific
value that random variable can take
▶Event where random variable Xtakes value x:
X= x
Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Random Variable Probability Distribution SA: W03 17 / 50Random variable: Not function Xis random, but only argument ω:
▶Depending on outcome of random experiment ω, different value
x= X(ω)
▶Once ω is chosen, X(ω)is fixed, not random
xis also called a realisation of random variable X

Playing cards: Realisation X= 11 corresponds to drawing an Ace
Dice: Realisation X= 8 corresponds to eye sum 8

For finite sample space: Probability distribution is a table

Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Random Variable Probability Distribution SA: W03 41 / 50Remarks
Expected value of a discrete random variable: Weighted mean of all
possible values, weighted by their probability of occurring
Expected value: Often also referred to as µX:
▶Index Xwill often be omitted if random variable is clear
Probabilities for all values x1,x2,. . .,xnequal: Expected value equal
mean of values
Variance is square of spread of value of random variable from
expected value weighted with respective weight
Standard deviation has same unit as X:Unit of variance squared:
▶E.g. Xin meters (m) measured: Var(X)in square meter (m2)
▶σ(X)again dimension meter (m)

Peter Büchel (HSLU W) Random Variable Probability Distribution SA: W03 43 / 50How are this definition and definition for mean and standard deviation
for random variable Xrelated?
Distinguish between them very carefully:
▶Arithmetic mean x:Calculated from concrete data: From
observations x1,. . .,xnaccording to formula above for xn
▶Expected value E(X):Theoretical value , which results from
model , i.e. distribution
Hopefully: Arithmetic mean xapproaches theoretical value µX=E(x)
for more and more experiments, provided data follow distribution of X
If this is not the case: Something is wrong with model (e.g. all sides
of die have not same probability to be rolled)

Each side has same probability of being rolled
Justified assumption because of symmetry :All sides equal

This is not realistic
No real die is completely symmetric, i.e. not all numbers are equally
probable
Can try to construct die that is very fair and all rolled numbers occur
with a probability of almost one sixth
But to do this exactly is not possible
